newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's April jobless rate rises.
newsitem.headline: Germany's April jobless rate rises.

text.p: Germany's jobless rate rose in April, throwing further into doubt its ability to meet economic criteria for the single European currency in 1999.

Figures from the Federal Labour Office released Tuesday showed that German unemployment rose by 8,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.299 million in April, maintaining joblessness around current post-war record levels.

While the politically sensitive unadjusted unemployment total fell to 4.347 million in April from 4.477 million in March, giving a jobless rate of 11.3 percent, economists called the figures disappointing and said they would increase pressure on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.

"The figures will put more pressure on the government, throwing their forecast for a 2.9 percent (ratio of 1997 budget deficit to gross domestic product) yet further into question," said Hans Guenter Redeker at Chase Investments.

With key tax revenue estimates due later this month expected to show a widening shortfall in German state finances, Redeker said the government would be forced into more unpopular cost-cutting measures to get close to the 3 percent deficit ceiling required to enter the single currency.

In western Germany, the number of people out of work on a seasonally adjusted basis rose by 6,000 in April to 3.016 million. Eastern Germany added 2,000 to unemployment rolls, reaching a total 1.284 million.
The unemployment data came amid other contrasting indicators on the strength of the economy.
Industry orders for March showed a greater-than-expected rise of 1.1 percent compared with February, boosted by a sharp 7.4 percent growth in the formerly-communist east Germany.
But economists were wary about extrapolating underlying growth in the economy from the figures, saying most growth was still coming from foreign demand for German goods.
"Exports are the driving force for the economy, not domestic demand," said Uwe Angenendt, an economist at BHF-BANK.
